# How to Send a Quick Voice Message to a Family Member's Echo with Alexa+

> **In short:** With Alexa+, you can record a short voice note on one Echo and have it play out loud on a specific other Echo in the house (or on a family member's Echo account), hands-free. Amazon says Alexa+ uses more conversational AI to handle the request, so you can describe who and where naturally instead of memorizing exact commands.

Imagine you're downstairs and want to tell your partner upstairs that dinner's ready — but they're wearing headphones, or the kids are watching a show. A quick voice drop on the bedroom Echo solves it without anyone picking up a phone. This guide walks you through sending that two-second note to a specific Echo, naming the room or person naturally, and checking it actually landed.

## Before you start
- **An Alexa+ enabled Echo** in the room where you'll be speaking. Amazon says Alexa+ is rolling out to compatible Echo devices; if your Echo isn't on the list yet, the older "Drop In" workflow still works but uses different wording.
- **At least one other Echo** in your home (or in a family member's home, if they've added you as a contact). Both Echos need to be signed into Amazon accounts that are linked through the Alexa app.
- **The Alexa app on your phone** (free, iOS or Android) — already installed and signed in, with both Echo devices named clearly (for example: "Kitchen Echo", "Bedroom Echo").
- **Both people must have enabled communications** in the Alexa app. The default is usually on, but if messaging was ever turned off, you'll need to flip it back on.
- **About 5 minutes** the first time, including the app check; under 30 seconds once you've done it a few times.
- A quick honest note on what this **cannot** do: Alexa+ voice messaging is short and one-shot — it isn't a back-and-forth voice call, and it won't show up as a transcript if the recipient is away from the Echo.

## Step 1 — Make sure both Echos are named so Alexa can tell them apart
Open the **Alexa app** on your phone and tap **Devices** at the bottom (it usually has a small speaker or chip icon). You'll see a list of every Echo on your account. If two devices are both called "Echo" or "Living Room," tap one and choose **Edit Name** to give it something specific — "Kitchen Echo" and "Bedroom Echo" work well.
💬 Example name pair: "Kitchen Echo" and "Upstairs Echo."
**If it looks different:** some accounts land on a Devices page with a "All Devices" button first — tap that, then pick the Echo to rename. If you don't see a rename option, your Echo may not be on the Alexa+ rollout yet.
You'll know it worked when both Echos appear in the app with clearly different, room-based names.

## Step 2 — Confirm the recipient is in your Alexa contacts
Still in the Alexa app, tap **Communicate** at the bottom (it looks like two speech bubbles or a chat icon). Tap **Contacts** at the top of that screen. Find the family member you want to send to — they should already be there if you've ever called or messaged them through Alexa. If not, tap **Add Contact** and follow the prompts to add them by name or email.
💬 Example: add "Mom" with her Amazon account email so her Echo shows up under that name.
**If it looks different:** on some accounts the Communicate tab is labeled **Talk** or **Message** — the icon is the same. If you only see your own devices and no contacts, communications may be turned off in Settings → Alexa Account → Alexa Communications.
You'll know it worked when you can see the family member's name (and at least one of their Echo devices) listed under your contacts.

## Step 3 — Send a voice drop by speaking to your Echo
Walk over to the Echo you want to send **from** and say the wake word — usually "Alexa" — followed by your request in plain language. Alexa+ is designed to understand more conversational phrasing than the older Alexa, so you can describe the destination naturally rather than memorize a rigid command.
💬 Example phrases: "Alexa, drop a voice message on the Kitchen Echo." / "Alexa, send a voice message to Mom's Echo saying dinner is ready." / "Alexa, tell the Bedroom Echo we'll leave in five minutes."
**If it looks different:** if you only have one Echo in your home, Alexa may say she can't find the device you named — go back to Step 1 and make sure the names match what you actually said. If the older "Drop In" wording is what your Echo understands, that still works; the two-second voice note behaves the same way.
You'll know it worked when Alexa confirms out loud with something like "Sending your message to the Kitchen Echo" — then a short chime plays to show your recording has started.

## Step 4 — Speak your two-second note, then pause
After the chime, just talk naturally — a short sentence is plenty. The recording window is usually a few seconds; silence ends it automatically. There's no "send" button to press; stopping talking is what sends it. Think of it like leaving a voice memo on someone's answering machine: short, clear, and you're done.
💬 Example: "Hey, dinner's on the table — come down when you can."
**If it looks different:** if Alexa keeps the recording going much longer than expected, just stop and wait — most Echos end on roughly two to five seconds of silence. If the message cuts off too early, try again in Step 3 and speak a little faster, or break it into two shorter messages.
You'll know it worked when Alexa says something like "Message sent" and the Echo's light ring returns to its normal idle color.

## Step 5 — Check on the receiving Echo (optional but useful)
If you're curious whether it landed, walk to the other Echo and check the **Alexa app → Communicate → Recent**. Your voice drop should appear with the recipient Echo's name and the time it was sent. On the receiving Echo itself, the message plays out loud automatically when it arrives; the light ring pulses while it's playing so anyone nearby knows a message just dropped.
💬 Example: send "Test from the kitchen" first when you're setting this up, then walk upstairs and confirm you heard it.
**If it looks different:** if the recipient Echo is muted or "Do Not Disturb" is on, the message still arrives in the Alexa app but won't play out loud on the device. Tap the Echo in the app and check the **Do Not Disturb** toggle if you suspect this.
You'll know it worked when the recipient Echo announces your message in its own voice, or when the entry shows up in your Recent list with the right device name.

## Common mistakes
- **Both Echos have the same name.** If everything is just "Echo," Alexa can't tell them apart and will either ask a clarifying question or send to the wrong one. Rename each device with its room (Step 1).
- **The recipient isn't in your contacts.** You can only send a voice message to someone who has accepted your contact request in the Alexa app. Add them through Communicate → Contacts first, then have them accept on their end.
- **"Do Not Disturb" is on the receiving Echo.** The message still arrives but stays silent. Turn off Do Not Disturb in the Alexa app or by saying "Alexa, turn off Do Not Disturb" on that specific Echo.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** a quick voice drop replaces the "yell upstairs" routine, the "send a text" friction, and the "find my phone" scramble. It's also handy for relatives who prefer talking to typing — kids, older parents, anyone who'd rather hear your voice than read a message.
- **For your business or work:** if you run a small home business, you can drop a voice note from your office Echo to a workshop or garage Echo without leaving what you're doing — useful when your hands are full or you're mid-task.
- **If you want to go further:** try chaining voice drops with routines. In the Alexa app, create a Routine that, when you say "Alexa, family dinner," sends a voice message to a chosen Echo *and* plays a short chime — one phrase, multiple actions.

## Try it now
Pick two Echos in your home, give them clear room names in the Alexa app, and send one two-second test message between them. Time yourself — most people land their first successful drop in under a minute once the names are set.
